clue.text: Dance round home gym backward

indicators.note: Something written backward runs from its end to its start, so the letters named just before it go in the other way round.

parts.note: a round drawn on the page is the letter O
a bird's home is its nest
gym on a British school timetable is PE, here turned round

explanation.surface: Dancing in circles round a home gym, and then in reverse.
explanation.walkthrough: A nest is a bird's home, and PE is what a British school timetable calls gym. The dance is a ballroom number from the ragtime years, one pace to each beat of a brisk two-four.
explanation.definitionFit: The one-step is a ballroom dance of the 1910s, walked at one pace per beat rather than the waltz's three.

clue.text: Company overthrown by top U.S. Army figure?

indicators.note: To overthrow something is to turn it over, so the short word named just before goes into a down entry the other way up.

parts.note: Co is the company on a letterhead, overthrown to read OC
the word itself, dropped in whole
US is the standard short form of the United States

explanation.surface: A firm brought down by the most senior figure in the U.S. Army.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Army' wants to be the service the rest of the surface is full of; read it as arm-y and an eight-limbed creature arrives, which is what the question mark owns up to.
explanation.definitionFit: An octopus is the arm-iest animal going, with eight of them, so 'army figure' describes it once you stop hearing soldiers.

clue.text: Please go in vehicle right away

parts.note: to go in through a door is to enter

indicators.note: Something taken away is gone, so the letter named just before it is dropped from the word it was sitting in.

parts.note: a train is the vehicle
r is right on a map or a stage direction, and it is the letter that leaves the train

explanation.surface: Telling somebody politely to get into the car and set off at once.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Please' reads as the courtesy opening a request and is the verb meaning to delight. 'Right away' looks like one phrase meaning immediately, and is a letter plus the order to lose it.
explanation.definitionFit: To entertain guests is to please them, keeping a room happy for a whole evening.

clue.text: Lacking energy after tango and twist

indicators.note: A runner coming in after another finishes behind them, so the piece named first is entered second.

parts.note: tango is T in the radio alphabet pilots and police use
somebody lacking energy is weak

explanation.surface: The tango has left somebody with no energy for the twist.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Tango' and 'twist' both look like dances. The first is only its radio-alphabet letter, and the second is the definition, a small turn given to something.
explanation.definitionFit: To tweak a dial is to give it a small twist, both words carrying the same sense of a minor adjustment.

clue.text: A response about training period

indicators.note: To move about is to shift around with no settled place, so the letters named are rearranged.

parts.note: anagram fodder, nine letters

explanation.surface: A reply concerning the length of a training course.
explanation.walkthrough: 'About' reads as concerning, the innocent word of the surface, and is the instruction to shuffle. Football clubs use the answer for the weeks of work before the fixtures start.
explanation.definitionFit: The preseason is the block of weeks a club spends training before the fixtures begin, so it is a training period in the sporting sense.

clue.text: Shout at last shattered glass

indicators.note: A pane that has shattered is in pieces with none of them where it was, so the word named is rebuilt in a new order.

parts.note: to shout out is to cry out
the four letters of LAST, shattered into a new order

explanation.surface: Somebody finally shouting, having broken a window.
explanation.walkthrough: 'At last' is the surface's sigh of relief, and only the second of those two words carries letters. Glass of this kind is the fine lead sort a decanter is cut from.
explanation.definitionFit: Crystal is the clear lead glass that decanters and chandeliers are cut from, so 'glass' names the material.

clue.text: Young animals abandoning large underground areas

indicators.note: A crew abandoning ship leaves it behind for good, so the letter named next is dropped from the word before it.

parts.note: the young of cattle are calves
L is large on a clothes label, and it is the letter abandoned here

explanation.surface: Young animals deserting the big spaces below ground.
explanation.walkthrough: The animals are cattle: a calf is what the herd calls its young. 'Large' is the L of a clothes label rather than a word about the size of anything in the scene.
explanation.definitionFit: Caves are chambers hollowed out of rock below ground, so 'underground areas' describes them plainly.

clue.text: Very recently in the past you strayed carelessly

indicators.note: Work done carelessly comes out with things in the wrong places, so the word named is jumbled.

parts.note: 'you' in older English was ye
the seven letters of STRAYED, in a new order

explanation.surface: Somebody wandering off without paying attention, a while ago.
explanation.walkthrough: 'In the past' is not scene-setting: it tells you to use the old form of the word beside it, the ye of the King James Bible. The answer works as an adverb, which is how 'very recently' can define it.
explanation.definitionFit: Something that happened yesterday happened very recently, the phrase and the word both doing an adverb's job.

clue.text: Approximately under end of elephant's trunk

indicators.note: In a down entry what goes under something else is written after it, so the piece named first drops to the bottom.
The end of a word is the letter it finishes on, so take that one alone.

parts.note: the last letter of ELEPHANT
a hundred or so means approximately a hundred

explanation.surface: Something sitting roughly underneath the end of an elephant's trunk.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Trunk' is the elephant's nose in the surface and the body minus head and limbs in the answer. 'Approximately' is the two words 'or so', a swap crosswords lean on constantly.
explanation.definitionFit: The trunk of the body is what is left with the head and limbs discounted, which is exactly a torso.

clue.text: Friend climbing up to capture grand bird

indicators.note: In a down entry a word that climbs up is read from the foot of the grid towards the top, so the letters named go in backwards.

parts.note: a friend is a pal, climbing the down entry to read LAP
to capture a trophy is to win it
G is grand, the thousand of banknote slang

explanation.surface: A friend scaling something to catch a magnificent bird.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Grand' reads as admiration for the bird and is the single letter G. The friend is the crossword's pal, three letters that become something else as soon as the clue sends them upwards.
explanation.definitionFit: The lapwing is the crested green plover of British farmland, named for the lapping beat of its wings.

clue.text: Name of bird with large plumage in the back

parts.note: a tit is any of the small garden birds — blue, great, coal
L is large on a clothes label

indicators.note: Whatever is in the back sits at the rear, so take the letter standing at the end of the word named.

parts.note: the last letter of PLUMAGE

explanation.surface: A bird known for the big feathers at its rear.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Name of bird' invites you to look for a species, and it is really the definition plus the opening piece of the wordplay, with the split falling between the two words.
explanation.definitionFit: A book's title and a person's name are the same idea, the words a thing is known by, and both double as verbs for bestowing them.

clue.text: Listen in on what happens in "The Fall" after lead character goes missing

indicators.note: Something that goes missing is no longer there, so the letter named just before it is taken out.

parts.note: the Fall is what Americans call autumn, the season in which leaves drop
the leading character of that phrase is its L, and that is what goes

explanation.surface: Summarising a television drama now that its main actor has walked out.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Lead character' sounds like the star of the show and means the first letter. The capitals push you towards a series title when what is wanted is the American word for autumn.
explanation.definitionFit: To eavesdrop is to listen in on talk you were never part of, standing close enough to hear under the eaves.

clue.text: Peak rates upset flyers

indicators.note: A tray that is upset spills everything into a heap, so the letters named land in a new order.

parts.note: anagram fodder, nine letters

explanation.surface: Charges at the busiest time of day are annoying the customers.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Peak rates' is the phone bill or the hotel tariff, and the same words are nine letters waiting to be shuffled. 'Flyers' would rather be leaflets or air passengers.
explanation.definitionFit: Parakeets are the small long-tailed parrots now nesting wild in London parks, and like any bird they fly.

clue.text: Mushroom found in jalapeno kimchi

indicators.note: What is found in something is already sitting inside it, so the answer runs unbroken through the words that follow.

parts.note: running through jalapENO KImchi

explanation.surface: A mushroom turning up in a jar of chilli kimchi.
explanation.walkthrough: Both spicy words are there to make the surface a recipe, and the answer lies across the join between them, which is where a hidden word is hardest to spot.
explanation.definitionFit: Enoki are the long thin white mushrooms sold in clumps for Japanese soups and hotpots.

clue.text: A lot of shrimp and urchin

indicators.note: A lot of something is most of it and not all, so the word named gives up the letter at its end.

parts.note: scampi is the menu word for the big prawns, and all but its last letter is wanted

explanation.surface: A generous helping of shrimp, and a sea urchin besides.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Urchin' reads as the spiny thing on the seabed and means a ragged, mischievous child. Scampi is what a British pub menu calls large prawns, usually in breadcrumbs with chips.
explanation.definitionFit: A scamp is a cheeky, mischievous child — the street urchin of Victorian novels rather than the creature in the rock pool.

clue.text: Apple reduced price abroad for piece of office equipment

indicators.note: A price reduced comes down at the end, so the word named loses its final letter.
Letters sent abroad end up scattered far from home, so the ones named are rearranged.

parts.note: anagram fodder, five letters
PRICE reduced by its last letter, four more letters of fodder

explanation.surface: Apple cutting the price of its office supplies in foreign markets.
explanation.walkthrough: The capital letter makes Apple the computer firm and the surface a press release, though the fruit spells the same. 'Abroad' is the shuffle rather than a hint about imports.
explanation.definitionFit: A paper clip is the bent loop of wire every desk drawer keeps for holding sheets together.

clue.text: Wrapping up small bundle containing tail of striped fish

indicators.note: A box containing something has it inside, so the letter named next goes within the word before it.

parts.note: S is small on a clothes label

indicators.note: A creature's tail is its back end, so take the final letter of the word named.

parts.note: a wad of notes is a bundle of them
the last letter of STRIPED
the ling is a long cod-like fish of northern seas

explanation.surface: Packing up a small bundle with the tail end of a striped fish inside it.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Wrapping up' is a baby in its shawl rather than a parcel at the post office. Ling is a name crosswords reach for whenever four letters of fish are needed.
explanation.definitionFit: To swaddle a baby is to wrap it up tightly in cloth, and both words are here in their -ing form.

clue.text: A river bank had traps close to shore, illustrating hunter's point?

indicators.note: A trap holds on to whatever walks into it, so the letter named next is caught inside the word before it.
The close of a word is where it finishes, so take the letter it ends on.

parts.note: the word itself, dropped in whole
R is river on a map
a bank of seats or of lights is a row of them
the word itself, opened up to take a letter
the last letter of SHORE

explanation.surface: A riverbank that had traps laid near the water, picturing what a hunter is getting at.
explanation.walkthrough: 'A river bank' reads as one stretch of the water's edge and is three separate pieces. The question mark flags the pun: the hunter's point is the flint on his arrow, not the case he is arguing.
explanation.definitionFit: An arrowhead is the sharpened point fitted to a hunting arrow, so the definition is literal once you stop hearing 'point' as an argument.

clue.text: Old American comedians working together

parts.note: the Incas ruled Peru long before any European landed, so an Inca is an old American
a hoot is anyone who makes you laugh, so comedians are hoots

explanation.surface: A pair of veteran American comics sharing an act.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Old American' wants to be a veteran from the States and is the Andean empire the Spanish found in Peru. A hoot is a person or thing that is hilarious, which is how the comics come out plural.
explanation.definitionFit: To be in cahoots with somebody is to be in it together, working as one and usually up to no good.

clue.text: One pecan crushed with head of round kitchen tool

indicators.note: A crushed tin has lost its shape altogether, so the letters named are rebuilt in another order.
The head of a word is the letter it begins with, so take only that.

parts.note: anagram fodder, eight letters
the first letter of ROUND, joined to the fodder

explanation.surface: Cracking a single pecan nut with the top of something round.
explanation.walkthrough: The nut paints the picture and supplies the letters at the same time. Nine letters is a lot of anagram to hold in your head, and the 3-6 enumeration is the help: a short word then a long one.
explanation.definitionFit: A can-opener is the kitchen tool kept in the drawer for getting the lid off a tin.

clue.text: Hunter who gives a damn about nothing!

indicators.note: To put something about a thing is to wrap it round, so the letter named next sits inside the word before it.

parts.note: to damn something is to curse it, so the one who gives a damn is a curser
nothing is written as the round O

explanation.surface: A huntsman who could not care less about anything at all.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Gives a damn' means caring in the surface and damning — that is, cursing — in the wordplay. Coursing is the old country sport of setting greyhounds after a hare, run by sight rather than scent.
explanation.definitionFit: A courser is one who hunts hares by coursing them with dogs, so 'hunter' is the plain description of the job.

clue.text: Unknown number in German boat

parts.note: algebra writes an unknown quantity as x, y or z
acht is German for eight

explanation.surface: An unidentified figure aboard a German boat.
explanation.walkthrough: The German is doing real work: what is wanted is a foreign word for a number, not a number written in a German way. 'Unknown' is the algebra class's x, y or z.
explanation.definitionFit: A yacht is a boat kept for racing or pleasure rather than for work.

clue.text: Playing outside is tiring

indicators.note: Children playing run about with no order to it, so the letters named end up somewhere new.

parts.note: anagram fodder, seven letters

explanation.surface: Playing out of doors wears a child out.
explanation.walkthrough: The whole clue is a sentence a parent might say, and one word of it is the definition. 'Playing' looks like part of the scene and is the shuffle instruction.
explanation.definitionFit: Something tedious wears you down by dragging on, which is the tiring the definition means rather than physical effort.

clue.text: Superior evening meal starting late

indicators.note: A word that starts late does not begin where it should, so its opening letter is left out.

parts.note: supper is the British evening meal, lighter and later than dinner

explanation.surface: Sitting down to supper rather later than usual.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Starting late' reads as an ordinary remark about the hour and is the instruction to begin a letter in. 'Superior' is meant in its positional sense, the one of two that is above.
explanation.definitionFit: The upper of two decks or two lips is the one above, which is what superior means before it means better.

clue.text: Softly lifted dead part of flower

indicators.note: In a down entry a word that is lifted is carried up the grid, so the letters named are read from the bottom upwards.

parts.note: p is piano, the mark a score prints for softly
the late Mr So-and-so is the dead one, and LATE is lifted up the down entry

explanation.surface: A dead flower head being lifted gently out of the vase.
explanation.walkthrough: 'The late' is how an obituary says dead, and that is the word being carried upwards. 'Softly' is the p printed under the stave.
explanation.definitionFit: The petals are the coloured leaves of a flower head, the part that makes the display.

clue.text: Charmed by European with desire in bed

indicators.note: What goes in something sits inside it, so the letters just named are planted within the word that follows.

parts.note: the word itself, opened after its first letter
E is European, as on a passport or a plug rating
w is the standard short form of with
an itch to travel is a desire to

explanation.surface: Won over by a European lying in bed full of longing.
explanation.walkthrough: An itch is a desire you cannot leave alone, and 'with' shrinks to the w of a hurried note. 'Charmed' reads as the polite thing said on being introduced and means spellbound.
explanation.definitionFit: To be bewitched is to be charmed in the older and stronger sense, under a spell rather than merely delighted.

clue.text: Pickle and cheese sandwiches back in fashion

indicators.note: To sandwich a thing is to put it between two others, so the word named first closes round the letter named next.

parts.note: brie is the soft French cheese

indicators.note: The back of a word is the end it finishes at, so take the letter standing there.

parts.note: the last letter of FASHION

explanation.surface: Cheese sandwiches are popular again.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Back in fashion' is an idiom in the surface and an instruction in the wordplay, pointing at the letter at the back of the last word. 'Sandwiches' is the verb, not the lunch.
explanation.definitionFit: Brine is the strong salt solution that vegetables and meat are pickled in, so 'pickle' names the liquid rather than the gherkin.

clue.text: Tent cut in the back with sword

indicators.note: What is in the back stands at the rear, so take the letter at the end of the word named.

parts.note: the last letter of CUT
the épée is the heaviest of the three fencing swords

explanation.surface: A tent slashed at the back with a sword.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Cut in the back' reads as the damage done to the canvas and is a letter-picking instruction. The épée is a crossword regular, four letters of sword with two accents the grid ignores.
explanation.definitionFit: A tepee is the conical hide tent of the Plains peoples of North America, so 'tent' names the kind of thing it is.

clue.text: Positioned select group around planet's second moon

indicators.note: To go around a thing is to close round it, so the letter named next lands inside the word before it.

parts.note: a vase positioned on a shelf sat there

indicators.note: The second of anything is the one after the first, so take the letter standing in that position.

parts.note: the elite are the select few
the second letter of PLANET

explanation.surface: A hand-picked crew stationed in orbit around a planet's second moon.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Planet's second' sounds like a second moon and is the second letter of the word PLANET. The astronomy of the surface runs right up to the definition, which is the last word of all.
explanation.definitionFit: A moon is a natural satellite, a body held in orbit round a planet, so the definition names the commonest kind for the whole class.

clue.text: Papa in old picture

parts.note: papa is P in the radio alphabet
a band that is in is hot, both words meaning the one everybody wants
o. is the dictionary's short form of old

explanation.surface: Father turning up in an old family snap.
explanation.walkthrough: The surface is a caption under something from the album, and 'Papa' is the radio alphabet's letter rather than the man. 'In' is not joining anything here: it is a word in its own right, and what is in is what is hot.
explanation.definitionFit: A photo is a picture made with a camera, the everyday short word for one.

clue.text: Fall back on side of ladder at recess

parts.note: a memo headed 'on the subject of' is marked re

indicators.note: A word's side is its outer edge, so take the letter standing at that end of it.

parts.note: the letter at the side of LADDER, its first
an apse is the rounded recess at the end of a church

explanation.surface: Leaning back against the side of a ladder during the break.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Recess' is the break between lessons in the surface and the church's rounded alcove in the wordplay. 'On' is the crossword's re, the word at the head of a memo.
explanation.definitionFit: To relapse is to fall back into an illness or a habit that had been left behind.

clue.text: Doctor having difficulties, missing medium bandages

parts.note: Dr is the doctor's title on a brass plate

indicators.note: A letter missing from a word is simply not there, so the one named just after this comes out.

parts.note: a run of messes is a run of difficulties
M is medium on a clothes label, and it is the letter that goes

explanation.surface: A doctor in trouble because the medium bandages have run out.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Bandages' sits at the end where a noun belongs and is the verb: a nurse dresses a wound. 'Medium' is the M of a clothes label, not a spiritualist.
explanation.definitionFit: To dress a wound is to bandage it, dressing being the word a nurse uses for putting the covering on.
